featuredReport.title: llm: add a provider cooldown registry and honour Retry-After instead of a constant retry backoff
featuredReport.summary: The issue proposes adding a provider cooldown registry and honoring the Retry-After header to improve rate limiting. Currently the retry mechanism uses a constant exponential backoff and ignores the Retry-After values sent by providers, leading to repeated attempts during rate limit windows. This feature will track per‑provider cooldown periods and respect provider‑specified retry delays.
featuredReport.suggested_next_action: Design and implement a provider cooldown registry that stores the time a provider hit a rate limit, and modify the retry loop to use the captured Retry-After value (or the registry) instead of the fixed backoff.

reports.title: plugins: enabled external plugins never activate on the one-shot CLI run path (hooks silently skipped, no error)
reports.summary: External plugins configured and enabled fail to activate during one-shot CLI execution, resulting in hooks being silently skipped. Direct calls to the plugin registry work as expected, but the `openminion run` CLI path bypasses plugin initialization. This prevents expected plugin hooks from executing without raising any warnings or errors.
reports.suggested_next_action: Investigate CLI runner initialization logic to ensure plugin registry configuration is properly loaded and activated before processing commands.

reports.title: self_improvement: max_applied_notes and min_token_overlap are accepted, persisted and never enforced
reports.summary: Two configuration settings in runtime.self_improvement (max_applied_notes and min_token_overlap) are parsed and persisted but never enforced by runtime consumers. Operators setting these values experience silent no-op behavior while a hardcoded context limit remains active. Enforcing these parameters in note ranking and context retrieval will resolve the inconsistency.
reports.suggested_next_action: Verify if a contributor PR is actively addressing this issue, and update context retrieval and ranking logic to enforce max_applied_notes and min_token_overlap.

reports.title: fix(storage): treat literal empty storage.path like omitted path (Refs #766)
reports.summary: The PR fixes a bug where setting storage.path to an empty string in agents.json caused the database path to resolve incorrectly, leading to sqlite3.OperationalError. It treats empty strings like None while preserving whitespace filenames and existing path handling, and adds regression tests and config bootstrap. An Unreleased note is also added to document the fix.
reports.suggested_next_action: Run CI for the storage module and merge once tests pass.

reports.title: [0.1.22] Agent.run(timeout_seconds=...) cannot extend the 300 s brain turn budget, and the budget stop is returned as a normal reply
reports.summary:
The Agent.run() timeout parameter is ignored - the turn stops at 300 seconds regardless of the timeout value passed, and returns a misleading stop message instead of raising a proper timeout error. This prevents users from extending the brain turn budget beyond the 300s default limit.

When using output_type=SomeModel, the issue surfaces as an invalid JSON AgentOutputValidationError instead of a clear timeout exception, masking the actual problem.
reports.suggested_next_action: Investigate the root cause in runtime.brain_turn_timeout_seconds handling and ensure Agent.run respects the timeout_seconds parameter passed by users

reports.title: [0.1.22] Runtime bootstrap fails on Windows (WinError 206) because browser-playwright artifact dirs are created under the CWD even when no browser tool is used
reports.summary: The runtime bootstrap fails on Windows when the current working directory path exceeds the MAX_PATH limit, because Playwright artifact directories are placed under the workspace root instead of the short OPENMINION_HOME path. This occurs even when no browser tools are enabled, causing the agent setup to abort with a WinError 206. The issue blocks Windows users from running openminion in deep project directories.
reports.suggested_next_action: Assign to the tools maintainer to adjust the Playwright artifact root handling to respect OPENMINION_HOME or allow explicit configuration, and add a test for long path scenarios on Windows.

findings.title: Bracketed IPv6 entries in NO_PROXY break every provider call with a misleading error

blocks.text: Repro: in this sandbox the environment ships NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1,[::1],[fd8b:...]. Start any agent run against a real provider.
Expected: the provider call goes through the proxy, or bypasses it for loopback only.

Actual: every call fails with Invalid port: ':1]' from httpx, which points at a port parsing problem in the user's own config, not at the environment variable. Removing the bracketed entries (or setting NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1) fixes it. Curl is unaffected, which makes the failure look SDK-specific when it is not.
Note: environment-specific, but the error message sends you to the wrong layer. A clearer httpx/SDK error would save real debugging time.

findings.title: Skill lifecycle: an ingested skill is invisible until admitted, and the errors do not say so

blocks.text: Reproduced end to end with openminion skill CLI against a project home:
skill ingest --file SKILL.md --name triage-rubric --scope project --trust trusted_local returns ok with a skill id and version hash, plus the warning admission.pending.

skill list then prints "No skills found". skill show, skill validate and skill debug for the same id all return NOT_FOUND ("Skill not found"), the same error as for a skill that does not exist at all.

The reason is only visible in the source (tools/skill/plugin.py::_model_visible_package): a skill is model-visible only when its scope is global (or agent-owned) AND the requested version is the admitted active version. Project scope is stored "as a label only" per the CLI's own JSON output, which the ingest success message does not surface as a warning.
Re-ingesting the same file with --scope global fails with SKILL_SCOPE_OWNER_CONFLICT until the first skill is removed.

skill admit with the ingest hash then fails SKILL_ADMISSION_VALIDATION_FAILED with blocker status.requires_verification; it only succeeds once --verification-check, --verification-result passed and --verification-evidence-ref are supplied, plus --expected-active-version-hash none for a first admission.
The version hash changes when only the scope changes (d39f44de... for project scope, 5684b201... for global), so the hash printed by a failed first ingest cannot be reused.
Expected: ingest output (or skill list) would show the skill as pending admission, and NOT_FOUND errors would distinguish "missing" from "exists but not admitted / not visible in this scope".

Actual: a successfully ingested skill is indistinguishable from a missing one until you read the plugin source. The full path (ingest as global, remove on conflict, admit with verification evidence) does work, and is documented in the README.
Minor: ingest also emits six parse.warning:h2_flattened_into_parent warnings for a plain ##-sectioned SKILL.md; harmless, but it reads like the file format is wrong when it is not.

findings.title: Chunked-streaming responses through a proxy relay make the provider layer report EMPTY_PROVIDER_RESPONSE

blocks.text: Repro: point the OpenAI-compatible provider at a loopback relay that forwards the upstream response as HTTP chunked transfer encoding (headers, then body chunks, then the terminal chunk). Run any agent.

Expected: the run proceeds; the upstream responses are valid OpenAI-shaped JSON with native tool calls (verified by replaying the same request shape non-streaming, which returns a correct tool_calls payload).

Actual: every agent run fails with ProviderError: EMPTY_PROVIDER_RESPONSE: Provider returned no usable entry response after configured retries, even though the relay log shows HTTP 200 for every request (5 attempts, then the run aborts). The identical pipeline through a relay that buffers each response and returns it with a Content-Length succeeds immediately.
Evidence: runs/run-01-failed-chunked-relay/ (summary and scan error), runs/relay.log.

Honest limit: we did not isolate which exact framing interaction (chunk boundaries, flush timing, header set) the adapter's streaming parser trips on; telemetry omits response content by design, which made this harder to pin down than it should be (see F4). The workaround is in production in repositter/relay.py.

findings.title: Telemetry omits the content needed to debug provider-response failures

blocks.text: llm.response telemetry events carry usage: {} and _telemetry_policy: {"sensitive_content": "omitted"}. For F3 there was no way to see what the adapter received or why normalization judged it empty; diagnosis required building a separate capture relay outside the SDK.
Expected: a debug mode that records at least the response shape (finish reason, presence of tool calls, byte counts) without bodies.
Actual: only the final error string survives.

findings.title: Typed outputs are fragile with small free models; the runtime's JSON recovery is narrower than it looks

blocks.text: The classifier subagent returned openminion: {\n"category": ...} (a prose prefix before the JSON object). Agent.run raised AgentOutputValidationError, even though the facade's _coerce_output contains a balanced-brace JSON extraction fallback; the model's JSON was also missing fields the prompt had not enumerated explicitly.

Mitigations that worked: enumerate every required field in the instructions with types, demand "ONLY one JSON object", and add an orchestrator-side salvage that extracts the first balanced JSON object from error.raw_text, re-stamps identity fields (number, kind, title) from the fetch (facts the orchestrator owns), and validates again. Salvages are flagged in the run's classify log.

Cost note: validation failures are retried inside the run before the exception surfaces, so a malformed-output problem silently burns several billable (or quota-counted) requests. Our first probe pair cost 14 requests for two tiny runs.

findings.title: memory.write requires confirmation by default; the fix is declarative but undiscoverable from the tool docs

blocks.text: memory.write is WRITE_SAFE with idempotent=False, so the policy engine classifies it as a write with unknown reversibility and the default action policy (require_confirm) pauses the run for a human OK. An autonomous agent that must ask permission to remember anything cannot complete a batch run.

Fix: an action-policy rule {"match": {"tool_name": "memory.write"}, "mode": "auto"} in agents.json. This works cleanly and is the right design (policy is data, not code), but nothing in the tool's own help suggests it; we found the rule format by reading base/config/parser/action.py and the policy module source.

findings.title: memory.write rewrites the record key without saying so

blocks.text: Instructed key: triaged:openminion/openminion#759. Stored key: fact:triaged_openminion_openminion_759 (type prefix added, : and / and # slugified away).

Consequence: any matching logic keyed on the exact requested key format breaks. RepoSitter's scan therefore matches on record content (which we now make name the full owner/repo explicitly) rather than on the key. Worth documenting on the tool: key normalization is reasonable, silent normalization is a trap.

findings.title: One agent run costs far more model requests than its visible tool calls

blocks.text: Measured with the relay log and a one-off capture of request bodies:
A scan stage (4 tool calls: skill.get, fetch, memory.search, plus the final answer) costs about 12 model requests.
A full 1-item run (scan, classify, record) cost 22 requests.

The extra calls are runtime-internal helpers, identified from their system prompts: a skill-selection helper (1 per run), a freshness-routing classifier (1 per run), a clarify helper, repeated batch guards, and, under the default tool_call_strategy: "hybrid", a separate "tool-calling contract" call per tool invocation (9 in one run). Switching the provider to tool_call_strategy: "native" removes the contract calls; the per-run helpers remain.

Impact: on OpenRouter's free tier (50 requests/day, failed requests count) the SDK's real cost per workflow is roughly 3 to 5 times the naive estimate. Anyone budgeting a free-tier agent needs the relay style request log; the provider's own usage counter is eventually consistent and lagged our relay count by several requests at times.
Suggestion: expose a per-run request budget and a breakdown of internal versus agent-visible calls in result.stats.

findings.title: memctl, the documented memory operator surface, fails out of the box

blocks.text: memctl forget --memory <id> and memctl search <q> both abort with FileNotFoundError: config file not found: <home>/memory.yaml. The runtime itself never creates a memory.yaml (the agent writes memory happily without one), so the operator CLI is unusable in exactly the layout the runtime produces.
Expected: memctl would fall back to the same defaults the runtime uses, or the runtime would write the config it expects.
Workaround used: none needed for the workflow (records are managed through the agent), but deleting a single record through a supported path was not possible during development.

findings.title: Default timeouts are hostile to slow models

blocks.text: Defaults found in scoping: 90 s chat turn cap (chat_turn_timeout_seconds) and a 60 s per-request preset for Ollama. Free-tier hosted models regularly exceed these under load. RepoSitter raises the turn caps to 600/900 s and the provider timeout to 300 s in config. First-time users will hit this as unexplained TurnTimeoutErrors.

findings.title: Config is anchored to the working directory and stores absolute paths

blocks.text: openminion setup/config init write .openminion/agents.json under the current directory's home, and the generated config embeds an absolute storage path. Moving a project means regenerating config; checking the generated file into a repo leaks machine paths. This repo therefore gitignores .openminion/ and ships config/agents.example.json with only the values that matter.

Related: a long-lived openminion.daemon process holds state across invocations; after changing config or environment, stale daemons can keep serving the old setup. We had to kill one during development.

findings.title: The classifier drifts outside the rubric's label vocabulary

blocks.text: Run 0's report for issue #759 suggested labels feature, rate-limit, retry, provider, performance. The rubric's vocabulary is bug, enhancement, question, documentation, needs info, good first issue, help wanted, duplicate, wontfix; the correct head label was enhancement. Category and priority were right, and the summary was accurate.

This is a model-quality observation, not an SDK defect. It is why RepoSitter treats reports as drafts for a human and never auto applies labels outside the approval gate. A schema-level enum on suggested_labels would catch it, at the cost of more validation retries (F5); we chose to log the drift instead.

findings.title: A repeated-tool-batch guard can interrupt legitimate multi-record writes

blocks.text: During the record stage the runtime injected "You have repeated an identical successful tool batch. Do not..." when the model re-issued a memory.write. Writing several similar records in one stage is the normal shape of this workflow; the guard's threshold is worth knowing about before designing batch writes. The stage still completed and the record landed (record id returned and later found by search).

findings.title: Smaller observations

blocks.text: Docs pin openminion 0.1.20; PyPI serves 0.1.21. We pinned and tested 0.1.21 and say so in requirements.txt.

The built-in github.* tools require a GITHUB_TOKEN environment variable. RepoSitter instead uses its own read tools plus a credential surrogate for writes, so no token sits in the agent's environment; worth copying for other builders.
Unauthenticated GitHub reads share the egress IP's 60 requests/hour budget (we observed 20 remaining at one point). Not an SDK issue; a deployment reality for agent sandboxes.

The Cortensor hackathon documentation still describes a dedicated submissions repository "to be added before kickoff" and a TBD deadline; in practice entrants publish their own repo and submit a DoraHacks Buidl. The event page's own text is the stale part.

findings.title: Provider economics forced a switch from OpenRouter to Gemini; the relay and config now carry both routes

blocks.text: Why: F8 measured one SDK run at 3 to 5 times its visible tool calls, and OpenRouter's free tier allows 50 requests a day with failed requests counting. On day 1 that cap ended run 02 mid-flight (RATE_LIMITED in the propose stage), and 3 of 5 classifications failed on the F5 prose-instead-of-JSON error from the small free model cohere/north-mini-code:free. The binding constraints were the daily cap and typed-output reliability, not the SDK.

Switch (2026-11-16, operator approved): the primary route is now Google's Gemini API free tier through its OpenAI-compatible endpoint (https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/openai), model gemini-3.6-flash, the model the SDK's own setup catalog recommends for its gemini preset. Gemini's free tier allows orders of magnitude more requests per day than 50, and a frontier class model is expected to end the prose-JSON failure mode. That expectation is stated as a hypothesis until a live run proves it (see the status below).

SDK shape worth knowing: there is no gemini runtime adapter and config init --provider does not accept gemini. The preset's runtime adapter is openai, so the Gemini route lives in the providers.openai block with provider_identity pinned to the gemini translation (service_vendor: gemini, model_family: gemini); without the pin, a loopback base_url makes the identity resolver report vendor unknown. The agent profile's provider is therefore openai on the Gemini route and openrouter on the fallback route.

What changed: repositter/relay.py is provider-parameterised (PROVIDERS map: upstream base, connector credential name, allowed hosts) and keeps the F3 buffered-response behaviour and the no-bodies logging discipline for both routes; the relay log now records the provider per request. repositter.toml carries [model] provider and the pinned model; run.py gained --provider. OpenRouter remains fully wired as the fallback (provider block untouched in .openminion/agents.json, one flag plus one profile value to return to it).

Smoke evidence (2026-11-16): a minimal SDK run (no RepoSitter tools, trivial prompt) against the Gemini config forwarded 15 requests through the relay to Google, all correctly addressed (POST /v1/chat/completions, model gemini-3.6-flash) and all answered HTTP 400 by Google. The wiring is proven end to end; the failure is the credential, not the plumbing.

Blocker: the stored custom.gemini credential is rejected by Google as not a valid API key (INVALID_ARGUMENT, API_KEY_INVALID) on the model list, on a chat completion probe and through the relay. Controls run the same day: the OpenRouter helper verified live through the identical surrogate mechanism, and a garbage bearer token produces Google's identical response. Remedy: reconnect custom.gemini with a valid Google AI Studio API key, then rerun the connector helper's models and probe and this smoke run before any pipeline run uses the Gemini route.

findings.title: An agent run can return success at the API level while doing nothing at all

blocks.text: Repro (2026-11-17, finish-day2 pass): the record stage was run as a standalone ops-agent run whose prompt was the pipeline's standard record prompt plus an appended "additional instruction" paragraph (asking for an origin note inside each memory record's content).

Actual: the run returned normally after 278 s and 4 LLM calls with tool_calls_count: 0 and the final text "I could not safely update the task conditions. Please restate the current task and its required conditions." (brain_status: waiting_user). No exception, no error artifact; a caller that only checks for exceptions records the stage as successful while nothing was written.
Retrying the same record with the extra instruction woven into the prompt's main sentence instead of appended after the report JSON worked first try (1 memory.write, record verified by search).

Lesson for SDK users: a stage's success signal has to include its tool-call count or a read-back of the effect, never just the absence of an exception. RepoSitter's finish-day2 driver was caught by its own verification stage here; the run-05 summary in runs/ documents the correction.

findings.title: The Groq route works, but Groq's free-tier tokens-per-minute limit collides with the SDK's request bursts

blocks.text: Wiring (2026-11-17, operator directed after the Gemini per-key 429 wall in the day 2 update below): the relay gained a groq route (upstream https://api.groq.com/openai/v1, custom.groq credential), and because the SDK ships a native groq adapter (an OpenAI-compatible provider subclass), the route lives in the providers.groq block of .openminion/agents.json with base_url pointed at the relay, model openai/gpt-oss-120b, tool_call_strategy: native, timeout 300 s, and the agent profile's provider set to groq. No provider_identity pin is needed on this route (contrast F15). repositter.toml, the ProjectConfig defaults and scripts/finish_day2.py (new --provider/--model flags, plus a memory read-back verification stage on its classify path, per F16) were updated to match.

Cloudflare gotcha: the first pipeline probe died with AUTH_ERROR ... groq auth failed: HTTP 403 on every request, while the connector helper worked fine. Reproduced directly: the same request with urllib's default user agent returns HTTP 403 with body error code: 1010 (Cloudflare refusing the client signature, as the custom.groq connector doc warns), and with the browser user agent the helper sends it returns 200. The relay forwarded no user agent; it now sends the same browser user agent as the helpers. The 403 is a signature refusal, not a credential problem; do not rotate the key over it.

The wall: with the user agent fixed, the pipeline probe (scripts/model_probe.py: a forced tool call, then a delegated classifier returning a typed TriageReport) got real completions through the full SDK + relay path (2 HTTP 200 among the first 7 requests) but then hit Groq's free-tier rate limit and died with RATE_LIMITED (the provider error names a tokens-per-minute limit for openai/gpt-oss-120b). Of the probe's 13 relay requests: 3 HTTP 400, 2 HTTP 200, 8 HTTP 429. Per this pass's stop rule, no further provider work was attempted, so the probe never completed and steps 2 and 3 below were not run on Groq.

Reading: the SDK fires its internal helper calls (F8) in bursts of several requests within seconds, each carrying the full system prompt and tool schemas. A per-minute token budget sized for chat use is spent by a handful of those bursts, where Gemini's limit behaved as a request-rate wall and OpenRouter's as a daily count. Any future Groq attempt needs pacing the SDK itself does not offer (throttling at the relay is the obvious seam: it already sees every request), or a paid tier. This is a provider-economics constraint, not an SDK defect and not a model-quality result: the two 200s show the model answering through the pipeline, but no classification was completed, so gpt-oss-120b's typed-output reliability for this pipeline is still unproven either way.

Unexplained: the 3 HTTP 400 responses that preceded the first 200 in the same probe. The relay does not log bodies (by design), so what Groq rejected is unknown. Recorded as an observation, not a conclusion.

findings.title: Relay-side pacing makes the Groq route survivable: a token bucket sized from Groq's own limit headers, plus bounded 429 absorption

blocks.text: Limit evidence (measured live on this account, 2026-11-17): a one-off diagnostic completion through the connector surrogate returned x-ratelimit-limit-tokens: 8000 (the tokens-per-minute cap for openai/gpt-oss-120b on the free tier) and x-ratelimit-limit-requests: 1000 (per day). The diagnostic used 78 prompt tokens with a 64-token completion allowance, and x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens fell by exactly 142, so Groq charges a request against the minute window at admission as prompt tokens plus the requested completion allowance. That is the number the F17 bursts were blowing: two SDK helper calls carrying a few thousand prompt tokens each spend most of the 8,000 in seconds.

Implementation (repositter/relay.py, GroqPacer, groq route only; the gemini and openrouter routes are byte-for-byte the old behaviour): before each send the relay estimates the admission charge as request-body bytes / 4 plus the body's max_completion_tokens/max_tokens (default reserve 1,024 when the SDK sets neither) and meters it through a token bucket of capacity 7,200 (90% of the measured 8,000) refilling at 120 tokens/second. A 2.2 s minimum interval between request starts also keeps the route inside the stated 30 requests/minute cap. After every response the bucket re-syncs down to the x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens header when one is present, so estimation error corrects itself instead of accumulating.

429 handling: a 429 is retried inside the relay instead of being handed to the SDK. The wait honours Retry-After, falls back to the x-ratelimit-reset-tokens duration, then to exponential backoff (5 s doubling, capped at 60 s), plus a 0.5 s buffer; bounded at 6 retries and 240 s of total wait per request so the SDK's own 300 s provider timeout is not consumed by waiting. If the bound is hit the final 429 is returned to the SDK unchanged.

Logging discipline kept: the relay log gains only numbers (attempt index, seconds paced, the rate-limit header values rl_limit_tokens / rl_remaining_tokens). Bodies, prompts and credential material are still never logged.

Offline verification: the pacer's arithmetic was unit-checked before any live run (charge estimation, a second 4,000-token charge waiting exactly (4000 − 3200) / 120 = 6.67 s against the refilling bucket, header re-sync clamping, and the retry-delay precedence Retry-After > reset-tokens > backoff).

Live verification (2026-11-17, scripts/model_probe.py through the real pipeline config): the pacing eliminated the rate limit entirely. The probe's 14 relay requests drew 7 HTTP 200 and 7 HTTP 400 and zero HTTP 429 (the unpaced probe in F17 drew 8 in 13), with 258 s of total paced waiting and the remaining-tokens header staying in the 4,100 to 6,500 range throughout. No 429 retry was ever needed. The token-limit problem is solved; what the probe then exposed is a model-output problem, below.

The probe still did not complete, for two separate non-limit reasons. Probe 1 (forced tool call) finished its run with tool_calls: 0: the model never called the forced tool, and the final text was a freshness-guard style refusal ("Missing live-data evidence for a freshness-sensitive answer"), not an answer to the probe task. Probe 2 (the delegated classifier) died with AgentOutputValidationError: the model returned openminion: { followed by otherwise well-formed TriageReport JSON, which is the F5 prose-prefix failure verbatim, from gpt-oss-120b this time. The plain connector probe (custom.groq helper) had returned clean JSON for the same kind of prompt, so the prefix appears when the model answers through the SDK's agent scaffolding, not through a bare completion. model_probe.py has no salvage path by design (it is the strict test); the production classify path in scripts/finish_day2.py does carry the F5 salvage, but per this pass's gate the leftovers were not run on a failed probe.

The 7 HTTP 400s remain unexplained, as in F17: the relay logs no bodies by design, so what Groq rejects in those requests is still unknown. They did not block the 200s and are recorded as an observation, not a conclusion.

findings.title: Groq's binding limit for this workload is tokens per day; a memory read-back by search is a ranked sample, not a census

blocks.text: Three observations from the 2026-11-17 finish pass on the paced Groq route, each evidenced first-hand:

The daily token budget is the real wall. After the F18 pacer eliminated the per-minute limit, the day's runs still died on HTTP 429, this time with x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens reading the full 8,000: the per-minute window was untouched, because the budget being spent was a different one. run-08-scratch's scan stage error named it directly, in Groq's own text: "Rate limit reached for model openai/gpt-oss-120b ... on tokens per day (TPD): Limit 200,000". Admission charges prompt tokens plus the requested completion allowance against that daily budget, so near the end of the budget a minimal request (5-word prompt, 16-token allowance; diagnostic at 12:24Z, HTTP 200, x-ratelimit-remaining-requests 940) is still admitted while SDK-sized requests are refused. Arithmetic: the day's four provider passes plus this one total roughly 170 relay requests, most carrying the full system prompt, rubric and tool schemas (F8); 200,000 tokens is a few hours of that traffic. The remedy is the 00:00 UTC reset, not pacing: pacing shapes the minute, it cannot stretch the day.

At least some of the F17/F18 HTTP 400s are the model inventing tools. A scan-probe run in this pass failed with Groq's own message surfaced by the provider layer: "Tool call validation failed: attempted to call tool 'exec' which was not in request.tools". gpt-oss-120b, answering through the SDK's agent scaffolding, sometimes emits a call to a tool that was never offered, and Groq rejects the whole request with HTTP 400. The relay still logs no bodies, so the share of the earlier 400s with this cause is unknown; the mechanism is now proven to exist and to occur in practice.

A single memory.search is not a read-back of the store. Run 06's record for issue #769 is present in .openminion/memory/memory.db (fact:triaged_openminion_ openminion_769, written 11:34:29Z, content matching the report verbatim) and in the FTS index, yet the finish-day2 verify stage's agent, searching "triaged openminion/openminion", reported it absent from its results. The recall layer returns a ranked set capped at 5 items and 500 tokens (PrecisionRecallOptions defaults in the SDK's recall module); five near-identical triage records compete for that budget, so any one search can omit a record that exists. F16's lesson extends: verify a write by reading the store (or by a search narrow enough to be a census), never by one broad search, and never by the writing run's own success signal.

findings.title: The F16 silent no-op recurred on Groq, and the run summary itself now carries the false ok

blocks.text: Repro (2026-11-18, run-09-scratch, Groq route): the record stage's ops agent returned the verbatim F16 refusal ("I could not safely update the task conditions. Please restate the current task and its required conditions.") with tool_calls_count: 0 and brain_status: waiting_user, after 3 LLM calls and 6 relay requests. No memory record for scratch issue #3 exists in the store (verified by direct store read: the only fact:triaged* keys are 759, 769, 779 and 780).

What is new versus F16: the refusal recurred on run.py's standard record prompt (report JSON, no appended instruction paragraph), so it is not confined to the appended-paragraph shape that F16 blamed. And the run's own summary.json records the record stage as "ok": true with the run id: triage.py sets ok unconditionally whenever the stage raises no exception (line 307). A caller that trusts the summary records the stage as successful while nothing was written, which is the exact trap F16 describes, now demonstrated inside the project's own summary artifact rather than only in a caller.

The same run's classify stage returned clean typed JSON for issue #3 with no salvage marker in the run artifacts, and the propose stage executed normally, so the refusal is specific to the record-stage agent run, not a route-wide failure. Consequence: a future scan of the scratch repo will see issue #3 as new again (no record), while the label read-back still proves the approval path end to end. The summary's record.ok needs the F16 check (tool-call count or store read-back) before it can be trusted; that fix is recorded here, not made in this run.
